concept.name: No demand
concept.definition: A price-volume indication, formalized in Tom Williams's Wyckoff-derived Volume Spread Analysis, of a deficit of buyers: typically an up-bar on narrow spread closing mid-range or lower on volume below that of the previous two bars. It signals that professional money is not interested in higher prices at that moment and warns of possible weakness ahead.
concept.intuition: The price ticks up but almost nobody is buying — a rally running on fumes.
concept.mechanics: The analyst flags narrow-spread up-bars (or down-bars making a higher high) with volume clearly below the prior two bars, then weighs the market background: near old tops or after signs of weakness, no-demand bars suggest shorts and exits from longs; after signs of strength, they may merely mark a pause. Confirmation comes from a subsequent down-bar on rising volume.
concept.failure_modes: Isolated low-volume up-bars are common in quiet sessions, holidays, and strong uptrends (where supply, not demand, is what is absent); acting on a single bar without background context is a known trap of the pattern.
concept.misconceptions: No demand does not mean price must fall immediately — in a strong background it often precedes only a brief rest — and the pattern is a process that can unfold over several bars, not a single-bar mechanical signal.
concept.example: Bitcoin grinds to 9,500 on volume half its average and closes mid-bar; the next day a high-volume down-bar begins a multi-week decline, validating the no-demand reading.

citations.source: VSA and cluster analysis. No Demand and No Supply (ATAS blog, describing Tom Williams's Volume Spread Analysis)
